business_outcome: Every contract request enters Legal complete, correctly triaged, and with a named owner for each ongoing obligation (renewal, termination, indemnity, security), so work moves faster and nothing important goes unmanaged after signature.
current_state_work_problem: 81.5% of the 2,400 contract requests arrive missing at least one required field, so Legal Ops spends days chasing requestors before real review even starts. Triage is inconsistent, obligations after signing have no clear owner (320 known gaps), and staff stitch information together by hand across many systems. Average request age is 31.6 days with a P90 of 52 days.
phase_one_solution_approach: Guided intake by request type that blocks incomplete submissions, an AI completeness and risk-triage check that routes each request to the right reviewer, AI-assisted obligation extraction that a human confirms, and an obligation-owner routing step. Attorneys keep all legal judgment; AI only prepares and organizes the work.

Phase one embeds in the existing contract system rather than standing up a new platform; broad build was explicitly rejected until baseline value is proven.
Cross-system obligation analytics depend on obligation data first being captured cleanly; premature to build the layer before the feed is trustworthy.

building_blocks_not_yet.reason: Whether to renew, renegotiate, or terminate is a business and legal decision; AI surfaces the deadline, humans decide.
Portfolio-level renewal analytics come after a clean, owned renewal record exists; not phase one.

This is a control and governance gap, not just a speed problem.
phase_one_solution_approach: An AI check that flags likely policy deviations against a defined policy standard and routes each flagged item to the correct approver with the relevant clause and policy reference, recording the decision. AI flags and routes; it never approves the exception itself.

use_case: Matter and outside-counsel intake and triage
business_outcome: Legal work sent to outside counsel is properly scoped, packaged, and triaged first, so only work that truly needs external review goes out, spend is controlled, and internal teams keep visibility over matters.
current_state_work_problem: Requests reach outside counsel with incomplete context, and low-value or triageable work is sent externally because there is no consistent internal intake and triage step. Outside-counsel avoidance is currently only directional, meaning the organization cannot yet see or control this spend systematically. This mirrors the same intake and triage weaknesses seen across Legal.
phase_one_solution_approach: A guided matter intake that captures scope and context, an AI-assisted triage that prepares a complete work packet and flags what can be handled internally versus needs outside counsel, and a human decision step where Legal approves the routing. AI prepares and recommends triage; attorneys decide.

building_blocks_not_yet.reason: Recommending legal strategy or handling approach is attorney judgment; phase one only triages and packages, it does not advise.
Outside-counsel spend analytics need a clean matter and invoice baseline first, which does not yet exist reliably.
Triage can be delivered on existing intake tooling; a matter-management platform build is out of phase-one scope.
Useful later to pull prior similar matters, but not essential to prove the intake-and-triage value in phase one.

Examples of matters that should not have gone to outside counsel
Current triage and approval practice for external legal work

business_outcome: Fewer invoices falling into manual exception queues across Lakeshore's operating companies, so shared-services AP clears invoices faster, captures more early-payment discounts, and reduces overtime and rework at month-end.
current_state_work_problem: A large share of supplier invoices stop for manual handling: purchase-order mismatches, missing goods-receipts, wrong tax or coding, duplicate submissions, and non-PO invoices routed to the wrong approver. Each operating company has slightly different tolerances and vendor master data, so AP analysts re-key, chase approvers, and email buyers repeatedly. The team cannot easily see which exception types are the biggest volume drivers or which operating companies and vendors generate them.
phase_one_solution_approach: Start read-only: categorize and rank exception reasons from real AP data, standardize match tolerances and coding rules across operating companies, and give analysts a retrieval copilot that assembles the PO, receipt, and prior-invoice context on one screen so they resolve faster. Automate only the safe, deterministic paths (clear duplicates, exact three-way matches within tolerance) with a human confirming before any payment-affecting action.

building_blocks_not_yet.reason: Recommending how to resolve a coding or matching exception affects payments and tax; needs a proven baseline and human sign-off before AI suggestions are trusted.
An agent that acts on exceptions is only safe after the deterministic automation and control gates are proven in phase one.

Three-way match tolerance rules per operating company
Vendor master and duplicate-detection rules
Chart of accounts and coding/tax rules
Current approver routing and non-PO handling rules
Volume and cycle-time by exception type and operating company
p2_current_state_focus: Quantify exception volume, mix, and cycle time by reason, operating company, and vendor; expose where tolerances, vendor data, and routing rules diverge; size the discount leakage and rework cost.
p3_solution_approach_focus: Design standardized tolerances and coding rules, the analyst copilot experience, and a decision tree separating auto-clearable paths from human-required ones; define the confirmation gate before any payment-affecting change.
p4_roadmap_value_focus: Sequence quick wins (duplicate suppression, clean three-way matches) ahead of harder non-PO redesign; build the business case on discount capture, reduced rework hours, and faster close.
p5_execution_focus: Run a weekly exception-reduction cadence: track first-pass yield, exception aging, and auto-clear rate per operating company; tune rules and expand automation scope as confidence grows.

required_controls: Human confirmation before any payment-affecting change
Segregation of duties between exception resolution and payment release
Full audit trail of every auto-cleared and reclassified invoice
Tolerance/rule change approval by controller
Duplicate-payment safeguard
what_good_looks_like: Exception rate and resolution time drop measurably, more invoices clear straight-through within tolerance, discount capture rises, and every automated action has a controller-approved rule and an audit trail — with analysts spending time on genuine judgment cases, not re-keying.

Dirty vendor master creating false duplicates or missed real duplicates
Operating-company rule differences treated as errors rather than legitimate variance
Over-claiming savings before discount capture is actually realized

business_outcome: Suppliers and internal requesters get accurate 'where is my payment' answers without an AP analyst manually researching each one, cutting inbound inquiry volume and freeing the team for higher-value work while improving supplier relationships.
current_state_work_problem: AP and shared-services mailboxes are flooded with payment-status questions from vendors and internal staff. Answering each one means an analyst looking across the ERP, the payment run, and email threads to reconstruct whether an invoice was received, is on hold, is scheduled, or was paid. Answers are slow and inconsistent, and the same vendors ask repeatedly because they have no self-service visibility.
phase_one_solution_approach: Deploy a retrieval copilot that composes a clear, plain-language status from trusted AP and payment data for an analyst to review and send, and stand up an internal knowledge base of standard responses. Automate only fully-resolved, low-sensitivity status replies (for example 'paid on date X, reference Y') behind a human check; keep any dispute, hold-reason, or bank-detail question with a person.

building_blocks_not_yet.reason: A full supplier self-service portal is a larger build; phase one deflects inquiries without committing to a new external-facing platform.
Governance is present but light-touch here; a heavier controls layer is only needed once outbound replies are automated at scale.

business_outcome: A faster, more predictable close across Lakeshore's operating companies, with fewer recurring issues, clearer ownership of blockers, and less last-minute firefighting by corporate accounting.
current_state_work_problem: The close is coordinated through spreadsheets, checklists, and email across many operating companies. Issues — late reconciliations, unexplained variances, intercompany mismatches, missing accruals — surface late and get tracked inconsistently. Corporate accounting cannot easily see, in real time, which entities are behind, which issues recur every month, and where the critical path is. Root causes are rarely captured, so the same problems repeat.
phase_one_solution_approach: Redesign the close as a tracked, structured workflow with clear owners, statuses, and dependencies; add an analytics layer that surfaces bottlenecks, recurring issue types, and at-risk entities; and give the close team a retrieval copilot that pulls prior-period notes and resolutions for a recurring issue. Keep judgment — accruals, variance explanations, sign-offs — firmly with accountants.

building_blocks_not_yet.reason: Suggesting accrual amounts or variance explanations touches the financial statements and audit; only appropriate after the tracked process and clean issue history exist.
An agent chasing or resolving close tasks needs a stable, well-owned workflow first, or it amplifies confusion during a time-critical period.

p4_roadmap_value_focus: Target the entities and issue types driving the longest close; build value case on days-to-close reduction, fewer late adjustments, and reduced overtime.
p5_execution_focus: Run the close on the tracked cadence; review recurring-issue trends and critical-path slippage each cycle; drive root-cause fixes so repeat issues decline period over period.

Automating coordination while leaving root causes unfixed

business_outcome: More reliable short-term cash forecasts across Lakeshore's operating companies, so treasury holds less idle buffer cash, borrows and invests more deliberately, and explains forecast misses with evidence rather than anecdote.
current_state_work_problem: Treasury builds consolidated cash forecasts from operating-company inputs of varying quality. Actuals routinely deviate from forecast, but the team cannot quickly attribute variance to its drivers — late AP runs, slipped AR collections, unexpected intercompany transfers, timing of tax or debt payments. Analysis is manual and backward-looking, so the same forecasting errors persist and treasury over-buffers to stay safe.
phase_one_solution_approach: Stand up an analytics layer that decomposes forecast-vs-actual variance by driver, entity, and category, and remediate the input data feeding the forecast so like is compared with like. Add a copilot to help analysts explain variance drivers from evidence. Keep the forecast itself, and any funding, borrowing, or investment decision, firmly human-owned; AI explains variance, it does not move money or set positions.

building_blocks_not_yet.reason: AI-suggested forecast adjustments or funding actions carry direct financial and liquidity risk; only appropriate once variance drivers are well understood and trusted.
Automating cash moves or forecast submissions is unsafe until input quality and variance attribution are proven; premature automation would propagate bad numbers.

required_p2_evidence: Historical cash forecasts vs. actuals by entity and category
Operating-company input methods and cadence
AP/AR timing data and payment-run calendars
Debt, tax, and intercompany transfer schedules
Bank balance and statement data
Documented forecast assumptions and known variance sources
p2_current_state_focus: Decompose historical variance by driver and entity; expose which inputs are unreliable and which categories drive the largest and most persistent misses; quantify the cost of over-buffering.
p3_solution_approach_focus: Design the variance-attribution analytics, the input-remediation approach, and the analyst copilot; define the strict boundary that AI explains variance and never proposes or executes cash actions.
p4_roadmap_value_focus: Prioritize the entities and categories with the largest recurring variance; build value case on reduced buffer cash, better borrowing/investing timing, and improved forecast accuracy.
p5_execution_focus: Review forecast accuracy and variance drivers each cycle; feed lessons back into input quality and assumptions; track buffer reduction as accuracy improves.
tower_metrics: Input timeliness and completeness by entity
Days of variance-analysis effort per cycle
required_controls: No AI execution of any cash, funding, or investment action
Human ownership and sign-off of the forecast
Auditable trail of variance analysis and input changes
Segregation between analysis and treasury execution
Approved data sources for bank and balance data
what_good_looks_like: Forecast variance is decomposed to its real drivers each cycle, input quality visibly improves, forecast accuracy rises, and treasury safely reduces idle buffer — with every cash decision still made by a person on better evidence.
biggest_risks_traps: Treating a variance-explanation tool as if it can predict or set cash positions
Bad operating-company inputs producing confident but wrong attribution
Reducing buffer too aggressively and risking a liquidity shortfall
Any AI path that could initiate a cash movement
gaps_in_current_moves_model: P2 variance decomposition needs granular forecast-vs-actual history with driver tagging that few clients hold cleanly; the model cannot manufacture it
P3 must enforce a hard 'explain-not-execute' liquidity boundary the model does not natively encode
P4 value (buffer reduction) requires a defensible liquidity-risk view the model has no way to represent, risking over-claimed savings

use_case: Duplicate and erroneous payment prevention (pre-pay controls)
business_outcome: Fewer dollars leaving Lakeshore in error — duplicate invoices, overpayments, wrong-vendor and fraudulent payments caught before the payment run rather than recovered painfully afterward — protecting cash and reducing recovery effort.
current_state_work_problem: Across operating companies with different vendor masters and approval habits, duplicates and overpayments slip through: same invoice submitted twice in different formats, PO and non-PO versions of one bill, fuzzy vendor-name variants, and occasional fraudulent or altered bank details. Today detection is partly after-the-fact via audits and vendor credits, and post-payment recovery is slow and incomplete.
phase_one_solution_approach: Remediate vendor master data, then add an analytics/controls layer that scores each invoice for duplicate and anomaly risk before the payment run, presenting flagged items to an AP reviewer with the matching evidence. All holds and releases stay human-decided; the system flags and explains, a person clears or blocks. No automated release of flagged payments in phase one.

building_blocks_not_yet.reason: Auto-releasing or auto-holding payments without human review is too risky early; a wrong auto-hold delays legitimate suppliers and a wrong release loses cash.
Recommending a pay/no-pay decision is a payment-integrity call that must be human-owned until detection accuracy and false-positive rates are proven.

required_p2_evidence: Vendor master with known duplicate/variant issues
Historical duplicate and overpayment recovery data
Invoice and payment-run history
Bank-detail change history and controls
Existing pre-pay control and approval rules
Known fraud or attempted-fraud incident records
p2_current_state_focus: Quantify duplicate/overpayment leakage and recovery lag; assess vendor-master quality and where variants hide; map current pre-pay controls and their gaps.
p3_solution_approach_focus: Design the risk-scoring and evidence-presentation experience, the reviewer workflow, and the control gates; explicitly keep pay/no-pay and hold/release as human decisions with tuned false-positive limits.
p4_roadmap_value_focus: Prioritize highest-leakage vendors and operating companies; build value case on prevented erroneous payments and reduced recovery cost, net of reviewer effort.
p5_execution_focus: Track prevented payments, false-positive rate, and reviewer throughput each cycle; tune scoring to protect suppliers from over-holding while catching real errors.
required_controls: Human decision on every hold and release
Segregation of duties between flagging, review, and payment release
Bank-detail change verification and dual approval
Audit trail of every flag, override, and clearance
False-positive threshold governance to avoid unfair supplier holds
what_good_looks_like: Risky payments are flagged with clear evidence before money moves, a reviewer decides every hold and release, prevented-loss dollars are visible and rising, post-payment recoveries fall, and legitimate suppliers are rarely delayed by false positives.
biggest_risks_traps: False positives holding legitimate suppliers and damaging relationships
Missing a real duplicate because vendor variants weren't reconciled
Over-trusting the score and letting a human rubber-stamp releases
Any automation that releases a flagged payment without review
Fraud adapting faster than the rules
gaps_in_current_moves_model: P2 leakage sizing depends on recovery and near-miss data clients rarely capture cleanly; the model cannot infer it
P3 must model a strict pre-pay human-decision gate and a false-positive tolerance the current model does not express as a first-class control
P4 prevented-loss value is inherently a 'losses avoided' number that is harder to bank and easy to over-claim, and the model gives little guidance on defending it

business_outcome: Cut the volume and cost of routine IT tickets across Lakeshore's operating companies by letting employees self-resolve common requests (password issues, VPN, software install, how-to questions) with a trusted assistant, freeing service desk agents for complex work and shortening wait times.
current_state_work_problem: Each operating company runs its own service desk with inconsistent tooling and knowledge. A large share of tickets are repetitive, low-complexity questions already answered somewhere in scattered runbooks, intranet pages, and agents' heads. Employees can't find answers, so they open tickets; agents copy-paste the same responses; knowledge is stale and duplicated across companies.
phase_one_solution_approach: Stand up a knowledge assistant that answers the top repetitive question categories using vetted, current IT knowledge content, with clear handoff to a human agent when it is unsure or the issue is sensitive. Start read-only and advisory: it suggests answers and self-service steps, it does not change any system on the employee's behalf yet.

building_blocks_not_yet.reason: Auto-executing fixes (e.g., resetting passwords or provisioning) crosses into changing live systems; not safe until deflection accuracy and knowledge quality are proven and identity controls are wired in.
Consolidating operating companies onto one service desk platform is a larger program; Phase 1 rides on existing tools to prove value fast.

required_p2_evidence: 12 months of ticket history categorized by topic, volume, resolution time, and reopen rate across operating companies
Inventory of current knowledge sources (runbooks, intranet, macros) with owner and last-updated date
Top 20 repetitive request categories and their current fully-loaded handling cost
Baseline first-contact resolution and average handle time per company
List of question types that must always route to a human (security, HR-adjacent, executive)
p2_current_state_focus: Quantify how many tickets are genuinely deflectable, where the answers already live, how stale and fragmented the knowledge is, and which categories carry the most repetitive load and cost per operating company.
p3_solution_approach_focus: Design the answer scope (which categories are in-bounds), the confidence threshold for handing off to a human, the knowledge-refresh model, and the employee experience across companies with different tooling.
p4_roadmap_value_focus: Build the deflection business case: expected deflection rate per category, agent hours freed, phased rollout by operating company, and the knowledge-maintenance operating cost that must be funded to keep it accurate.
p5_execution_focus: Run a weekly cadence on deflection rate, answer accuracy, escalation quality, and employee satisfaction; retire and refresh stale knowledge; expand category coverage only as accuracy holds.
tower_metrics: Deflection rate (share of eligible tickets self-resolved)
Cost avoided per month from deflected tickets
required_controls: Answers restricted to vetted, owned knowledge sources with visible citations
Guaranteed human handoff for security, HR-adjacent, and low-confidence cases
No account or system changes performed automatically in Phase 1
Content review and freshness owner for every knowledge source
Audit trail of what was answered and where the employee went next
what_good_looks_like: Employees get an accurate, cited answer in seconds for common issues, ticket volume for repetitive categories drops measurably, agents spend their time on complex work, and knowledge stays current because ownership and a refresh cadence are funded.
biggest_risks_traps: Confidently wrong answers erode trust and quietly increase rework
Stale knowledge poisons deflection; if no one owns refresh, accuracy decays
Deflection is claimed but tickets just shift channel or reopen later
Fragmented tooling across operating companies makes one experience hard
Measuring 'tickets touched' instead of genuinely resolved inflates the story
gaps_in_current_moves_model: No first-class notion of a funded knowledge-freshness owner as an ongoing operating cost
Deflection value is easy to overstate without a rigorous 'genuinely resolved vs. reopened' definition baked into value tracking
Model doesn't yet standardize a per-operating-company rollout ledger for holdco structures

business_outcome: Make getting the right application access faster and safer: requests are understood, routed to the correct approver with full context, and granted only after human approval, reducing wait times and access-related audit findings across Lakeshore's operating companies.
current_state_work_problem: Access requests flow through email, tickets, and spreadsheets with unclear ownership of who approves what. Employees don't know what to ask for, approvers lack context to decide, and joiner/mover/leaver changes lag. The result is slow onboarding, over-provisioned access, and painful audits because entitlements and approvals aren't consistently recorded.
phase_one_solution_approach: Assist and orchestrate the request-and-approval workflow without auto-granting. The assistant helps the employee request the right access, assembles context (role, manager, existing access, risk level) for the approver, routes to the correct approver, and records the decision. Every grant still requires an explicit human approval; high-risk and privileged access always escalates.

building_blocks_not_yet.reason: A full identity-governance platform rollout is a larger program; Phase 1 orchestrates and records on top of existing systems to prove flow and control first.
Introduced from Phase 4 once baseline cycle-time and audit-finding data exist; premature to run a value cadence before the workflow is trusted.

required_p2_evidence: Catalog of applications and their access levels, owners, and risk classification
Current request-to-grant cycle time and volume by application and company
Map of who actually approves what today vs. who should
Recent access-related audit findings and their root causes
Joiner/mover/leaver process documentation and current gaps
p2_current_state_focus: Expose how access is really requested, approved, and revoked today; where approver ownership is missing; how long grants take; and which gaps drive audit findings and over-provisioning.
p3_solution_approach_focus: Design the approval routing rules, the risk tiers that determine how much scrutiny a request gets, the context pack shown to approvers, and the strict boundary where automation stops and human approval is mandatory.
p4_roadmap_value_focus: Business case on faster onboarding, reduced over-provisioning, and fewer audit findings; phased by application risk tier and operating company, with the control model as a non-negotiable dependency.
p5_execution_focus: Track cycle time, approval quality, and access-review completeness; run periodic recertification; expand automation scope only for low-risk access as trust is earned.
tower_metrics: Share of requests routed to the correct approver first time
Over-provisioned / unused entitlements identified and removed
required_controls: No automatic granting of access in Phase 1 — human approval required for every grant
Mandatory escalation for privileged, financial, and cross-company access
Separation of duties enforced in routing (requester cannot approve own request)
Complete, tamper-evident record of request, context, approver, and decision
Least-privilege defaults and periodic recertification built in
what_good_looks_like: New hires get productive access quickly, approvers decide with full context, privileged access is always scrutinized by a human, and auditors can trace every grant to a documented, appropriate approval — with over-provisioning steadily shrinking.
biggest_risks_traps: Auto-granting access to move faster is the single biggest control risk — must not happen in Phase 1
Bad or missing application/role data makes routing and context untrustworthy
Separation-of-duties gaps let requesters approve their own access
Speeding up grants without also tightening revocation worsens over-provisioning
Holdco complexity: cross-operating-company access blurs approver ownership
gaps_in_current_moves_model: Model needs a strong, explicit 'automation stops here' guardrail concept for control-sensitive workflows so auto-grant never leaks in
Separation-of-duties and recertification aren't first-class control primitives yet
Cross-entity (holdco) approver ownership isn't modeled — real risk for shared services serving many operating companies

business_outcome: Resolve IT incidents faster by giving responders an accurate, up-to-date summary of what's happening and routing each incident to the right team the first time, reducing bounce-backs, mean time to resolve, and business disruption for Lakeshore's operating companies.
current_state_work_problem: Incidents arrive with sparse or noisy descriptions and get mis-routed between teams, each re-reading history and re-diagnosing. During major incidents, status is assembled manually from chat threads and calls, so leadership and affected businesses get inconsistent updates. Time is lost to triage and context-rebuilding rather than fixing.
phase_one_solution_approach: Provide a drafting and routing assistant: it summarizes the incident from available signals, suggests the likely owning team and priority, and drafts a status update — all for a human responder to confirm. It accelerates triage and communication; it does not take remediation actions or close incidents on its own.

building_blocks_not_yet.reason: Lightweight guardrails apply, but heavy governance tooling isn't the Phase 1 driver since the assistant only drafts and suggests — no automated remediation to govern yet.
Comes online in Phase 4/5 once mean-time-to-resolve and mis-route baselines are established; a value cadence before then would track noise.

required_p2_evidence: Incident history with descriptions, routing paths, reassignment counts, and resolution times
Current team-ownership map and routing rules across operating companies
Sample major-incident timelines showing how status was communicated
Priority/severity definitions and how consistently they're applied
Sources available at incident time (monitoring, prior similar incidents, runbooks)
p2_current_state_focus: Measure how often incidents are mis-routed and reassigned, how much time is lost re-diagnosing, and how inconsistent major-incident communication is today.
p3_solution_approach_focus: Design what a trustworthy summary must contain, the routing suggestion logic and confidence handling, the responder confirmation step, and the communication templates for major incidents.
p4_roadmap_value_focus: Business case on reduced mean-time-to-resolve, fewer reassignments, and faster, consistent stakeholder communication; phased by incident type and operating company.
p5_execution_focus: Track routing accuracy, reassignment rate, and resolution time; feed resolved-incident learnings back into summaries and runbooks; expand coverage as accuracy holds.
required_controls: Responder confirms routing and priority before action — no auto-close or auto-remediation
Summaries cite their source signals so responders can verify
Clear labeling that updates are drafts pending human approval
Sensitive incidents (security, data exposure) follow a protected path
Full timeline record of suggestions, confirmations, and communications
what_good_looks_like: Responders open an incident to a clear, sourced summary and a sensible routing suggestion, spend their energy fixing rather than triaging, and leadership gets timely consistent updates during major incidents — with humans still owning every decision.
biggest_risks_traps: A confidently wrong summary sends responders down the wrong path faster
Over-trust: responders rubber-stamp routing suggestions without checking
Security incidents mishandled if they aren't carved onto a protected path
Garbage-in incident data makes summaries and routing unreliable
Measuring 'summaries generated' instead of resolution and routing accuracy
gaps_in_current_moves_model: No first-class 'protected/sensitive path' concept for incidents that must bypass the standard assistant flow
Model lacks a built-in feedback loop that turns resolved incidents into improved future summaries and runbooks
Real-time / time-critical operating cadence differs from the model's periodic-review default

business_outcome: Reduce IT cost and risk across Lakeshore's operating companies by building a trustworthy view of every application — cost, usage, overlap, and risk — and identifying candidates to retire, consolidate, or renegotiate, with decisions made by humans on solid evidence.
current_state_work_problem: After years of acquisitions, operating companies run overlapping applications with no single, current inventory. Spend is fragmented across contracts, real usage is unknown, and redundant tools persist because no one can see the whole picture. Rationalization stalls because the evidence to decide is scattered and stale.
phase_one_solution_approach: Assemble and analyze a governed application inventory: bring together cost, usage, ownership, overlap, and risk into one intelligence layer, and surface prioritized rationalization candidates with the evidence behind each. Recommendations are advisory — retire/consolidate decisions are made by application and business owners, not automatically.

building_blocks_not_yet.reason: Nothing should be decommissioned automatically; retirement is a deliberate, owner-approved change with migration and dependency risk.
Consolidating onto target platforms is a downstream program that follows the rationalization decisions, not a Phase 1 activity.

required_p2_evidence: Consolidated application inventory across operating companies with owners
Actual usage/adoption data per application (not just licenses purchased)
Total cost per application including license, support, and infrastructure
Contract and renewal calendar with terms and exit clauses
Overlap map showing applications serving the same capability and their dependencies
p2_current_state_focus: Establish a single credible picture of what applications exist, what they truly cost, whether they're actually used, where they overlap, and what depends on them — replacing scattered, stale views.
p3_solution_approach_focus: Design the rationalization scoring (cost vs. usage vs. risk vs. overlap), the evidence pack per candidate, and the decision framework owners will use to choose retire / consolidate / renegotiate / keep.
p4_roadmap_value_focus: Build a phased savings roadmap tied to contract renewal timing and dependency risk, quantifying cost-out per wave and the migration effort each retirement requires.
p5_execution_focus: Run an ongoing operating cadence that tracks realized savings against the plan, keeps the inventory current, and re-scores the portfolio as contracts and usage change.
tower_metrics: Share of portfolio with current, trustworthy inventory data
required_controls: No application decommissioned without owner and dependency sign-off
Every recommendation traceable to its cost, usage, and risk evidence
Business-continuity and data-retention checks before any retirement
Inventory data governed for freshness and accuracy with named owners
Change and migration plan required before a retire decision executes
client_stakeholders: CIO / IT finance (technology business management) lead
what_good_looks_like: Leadership sees one trustworthy portfolio view, rationalization candidates come with the evidence to decide, retirements happen safely with dependencies handled, and realized savings are tracked against the plan rather than assumed.
biggest_risks_traps: Stale or incomplete inventory data leads to wrong retire decisions
Counting license spend without real usage overstates savings
Retiring an app that a hidden downstream process depends on causes outages
'Planned savings' declared as realized without a tracking cadence
Holdco politics: operating companies resist giving up 'their' tools
gaps_in_current_moves_model: Value tracking must distinguish planned vs. realized savings over time — easy to overstate at business-case stage
Dependency-risk modeling (what breaks if we retire this) isn't a first-class element
Cross-operating-company ownership and politics of shared/duplicated apps aren't modeled
Inventory freshness needs a funded ongoing owner, not a one-time data pull

business_outcome: Ensure every new hire is productive on day one and every departure is fully and promptly de-provisioned, by coordinating the many IT tasks behind joiner/mover/leaver events across Lakeshore's operating companies — cutting onboarding delays and closing the security gap left by incomplete offboarding.
current_state_work_problem: Onboarding and offboarding IT tasks (accounts, equipment, application access, group memberships) are tracked in checklists and emails that vary by operating company. New hires wait on missing access; more dangerously, leavers keep access for days or weeks because de-provisioning steps are missed, creating security and audit exposure. No one has a live view of completion.
phase_one_solution_approach: Orchestrate and track the joiner/mover/leaver task set from the HR trigger: the assistant generates the right task list per role and company, routes each task to the right owner, and tracks completion, flagging anything overdue — especially offboarding steps. Sensitive de-provisioning is executed by owners with confirmation, not silently automated, in Phase 1.

building_blocks_not_yet.reason: Phase 1 is mostly deterministic orchestration of known tasks; richer recommendation logic (e.g., role-based access suggestions) is a later enhancement.
A unified HR-to-IT provisioning platform across operating companies is a larger downstream program; Phase 1 coordinates across existing systems.

required_p2_evidence: Current joiner/mover/leaver task lists per role and operating company with owners
Time-to-productive-access for recent hires and gaps encountered
Time-to-full-deprovision for recent leavers and any lingering-access findings
HR trigger data quality and timeliness (are IT events fired reliably?)
Audit findings related to orphaned accounts or excess retained access
p2_current_state_focus: Show how long onboarding really takes, how reliably offboarding completes, where tasks fall through the cracks, and how big the lingering-access security gap is across operating companies.
p3_solution_approach_focus: Redesign the joiner/mover/leaver task flow, define role-and-company task templates, set ownership and escalation for overdue tasks, and fix the boundary where sensitive de-provisioning requires confirmed human execution.
p4_roadmap_value_focus: Business case on faster onboarding, eliminated lingering access, and reduced audit exposure; phased by operating company and by event type, with HR-trigger reliability as a key dependency.
p5_execution_focus: Track onboarding completeness, offboarding timeliness, and overdue-task rates; run recurring reviews to catch orphaned accounts; tighten automation for low-risk steps as trust grows.
tower_metrics: Time to productive access for new hires
Time to full de-provisioning for leavers
Offboarding completeness (share of leavers fully de-provisioned on time)
required_controls: Sensitive de-provisioning confirmed and recorded by an accountable owner, not silently automated in Phase 1
Hard escalation on overdue offboarding steps for departing employees
Complete audit trail linking each HR event to its completed IT tasks
Separation of duties between requesting and executing sensitive changes
Reliable, timely HR trigger as a governed dependency
client_stakeholders: IT service desk and provisioning teams
what_good_looks_like: A new hire has the right accounts, equipment, and access on day one; when someone leaves, all access is closed the same day with a clean audit trail; and leadership sees live completion status rather than discovering gaps at audit time.
biggest_risks_traps: Offboarding is the real risk: missed de-provisioning leaves live access for departed employees
Unreliable or late HR triggers mean the whole flow starts on bad data
Auto-executing sensitive de-provisioning without confirmation could disrupt the wrong person
Per-company task variation makes one orchestration model hard to standardize
Focusing on shiny onboarding while under-investing in unglamorous offboarding controls
gaps_in_current_moves_model: Model needs to treat an external trigger (HR event) reliability as a governed dependency, not an assumption
Time-critical offboarding SLAs differ from the model's periodic-review cadence default
Per-operating-company task-template variation isn't a first-class concept for holdco shared services
Separation of duties between requesting and executing sensitive changes isn't a built-in control primitive

business_outcome: New suppliers to Lakeshore's operating companies are onboarded faster and with consistent risk screening, so corporate shared services reduce onboarding cycle time and cut the number of high-risk vendors entering the base without proper review.
current_state_work_problem: Each operating company intakes vendors its own way, often by email and spreadsheet. Risk checks (financial health, insurance, sanctions/watchlist, cyber, conflict of interest) are inconsistent, and shared services can't see one clean picture of who is being onboarded, how long it takes, or which checks were skipped. Duplicate vendor records proliferate across operating companies.
phase_one_solution_approach: Stand up one intake front door and a standardized risk-review checklist for corporate shared services, with a copilot that drafts the risk summary from submitted documents and screening results. A procurement analyst always reviews and signs off before a vendor is approved. No auto-approval in phase one.

building_blocks_not_yet.reason: Full straight-through automation of approvals is unsafe until the standardized checklist and human review are proven stable; automate routing only after the manual path is trusted.
Replacing or consolidating vendor master systems across operating companies is a large program; phase one runs on top of existing systems rather than replacing them.
Deep vendor-master de-duplication across all operating companies is a heavy remediation effort better scoped as its own move once intake is standardized.

required_p2_evidence: Current intake volumes and cycle time per operating company
Existing risk-check steps and which are actually performed today
Sample of recent vendor onboardings with documents and outcomes
List of screening data sources available (financial, sanctions, cyber) and their coverage
Count and examples of duplicate vendor records across operating companies
p2_current_state_focus: Map how each operating company intakes and screens vendors today, quantify cycle time and rework, and identify where risk checks are inconsistent or skipped.
p3_solution_approach_focus: Design the single intake form, the standardized risk checklist, the copilot-drafted risk summary, and the review/approval workflow with clear human sign-off points.
p4_roadmap_value_focus: Build the business case on cycle-time reduction, fewer high-risk vendors admitted, and analyst time saved; sequence rollout operating-company by operating-company.
p5_execution_focus: Run the standardized intake live for pilot operating companies, track sign-off quality, and hold a regular operating cadence on onboarding volume, risk flags, and exceptions.

Number of high-risk vendors flagged before approval
required_controls: Mandatory human sign-off before any vendor is approved
Audit trail of every screening result and reviewer decision
Segregation between the analyst who prepares and the approver who signs off
Handling rules for sensitive supplier financial and personal data
Escalation path for high-risk or watchlist matches
client_stakeholders: Corporate VP of Procurement / Shared Services
what_good_looks_like: One clean intake front door where any operating company submits a vendor, a consistent risk summary is drafted in minutes, an analyst reviews and signs off, and shared services can see onboarding volume, cycle time, and risk flags in one place.
biggest_risks_traps: Screening data sources may be incomplete or stale, giving false comfort on risk
Operating companies resist a central front door and keep shadow intake processes
Copilot risk summaries could be over-trusted and reduce genuine analyst scrutiny
Duplicate and messy vendor data undermines a clean single view
gaps_in_current_moves_model: Moves model does not yet specify how external screening data sources are connected and their coverage verified
No built-in pattern for a de-duplication effort that runs alongside a live intake process
Limited guidance on how the copilot's confidence is shown so reviewers don't over-trust it

business_outcome: Statements of work across operating companies are reviewed faster and hold to Lakeshore's standard terms, so corporate shared services reduce off-standard clauses, contain unpriced scope, and lower contract risk before signature.
current_state_work_problem: SOWs arrive in many formats and are reviewed manually by whoever is available. Standard terms (rate cards, liability, data protection, deliverable acceptance) are enforced inconsistently. Reviewers miss non-standard clauses and scope that isn't tied to a price, and there is no easy way to see how often SOWs deviate from policy.
phase_one_solution_approach: A review copilot reads a submitted SOW, compares it against Lakeshore's standard-terms playbook, and drafts a flag list of deviations and missing clauses for a procurement or legal reviewer. The reviewer decides; the tool never approves or edits the contract on its own. Ties into AbarVa's Source surface where the SOW originates from a sourcing event.

building_blocks_not_yet.reason: Auto-routing and auto-clearing of clean SOWs should wait until the deviation-flagging quality is proven against reviewer judgment.
Deep integration into a contract lifecycle system is a later step; phase one works from submitted documents.
A regular value cadence is valuable but secondary until the review flow itself is trusted; add once deviation rates are measurable.

required_p2_evidence: Lakeshore's current standard-terms playbook and rate-card policy
Sample of recent SOWs across operating companies with review notes
Typical review turnaround time and reviewer workload
Examples of past disputes or overruns traced to weak SOW terms
How SOWs connect to sourcing events in Source today

p3_solution_approach_focus: Design the standard-terms playbook the copilot checks against, the deviation flag format, and the reviewer decision workflow with legal escalation.
p4_roadmap_value_focus: Justify the move on faster review turnaround, fewer off-standard clauses signed, and reduced unpriced scope; sequence by SOW volume per category.
p5_execution_focus: Run copilot-assisted review live for pilot categories, track reviewer agreement with flags, and refine the playbook based on real deviations.

Number of off-standard clauses caught before signature
Value of unpriced scope identified and closed
required_controls: Human reviewer decision required on every flagged deviation
Legal escalation path for high-risk clauses
Version-controlled standard-terms playbook with owner
Audit trail linking each flag to a reviewer decision
Confidentiality handling for supplier contract terms
client_stakeholders: Corporate VP of Procurement / Shared Services
what_good_looks_like: A reviewer opens a SOW and immediately sees a clear, cited list of where it deviates from Lakeshore's standard terms and what scope isn't priced, decides quickly, and shared services can see deviation rates across operating companies.

An outdated standard-terms playbook produces misleading flags
Reviewers may rubber-stamp the flag list instead of exercising judgment
Legal may distrust the tool without clear evidence of accuracy
gaps_in_current_moves_model: Moves model lacks a clear pattern for keeping the standard-terms playbook current and owned
No defined handoff between Source sourcing events and SOW review beyond narrative
Limited guidance on measuring copilot flag accuracy against legal judgment over time

business_outcome: Lakeshore's corporate shared services see every upcoming contract renewal across operating companies early enough to act, so fewer contracts auto-renew unmanaged, more are competitively sourced or renegotiated, and savings are captured that would otherwise be lost.
current_state_work_problem: Renewal dates live scattered in spreadsheets, inboxes, and individual heads across operating companies. Contracts frequently auto-renew because no one saw the deadline in time, forfeiting the chance to renegotiate or re-source. There is no single forward-looking view of the renewal pipeline or its value at stake.
phase_one_solution_approach: Build one consolidated renewal calendar and an intelligence layer that surfaces upcoming renewals ranked by value and negotiation leverage, with recommended actions (renegotiate, re-source, consolidate, let lapse). A procurement lead decides on each; the tool recommends but never triggers a renewal or notice on its own. Feeds candidates into AbarVa's Source surface for competitive events and Tower for value tracking.

building_blocks_not_yet.reason: Automatically issuing renewal or non-renewal notices carries real contractual and financial consequences and must stay a human decision in phase one.
A negotiation copilot is valuable later but depends first on a clean, complete renewal dataset; sequence it after the pipeline view is trusted.
Governance controls are lighter here than in intake or SOW review; add formal controls once actions on renewals are taken at scale.

Annual spend and value at stake per contract
History of contracts that auto-renewed unmanaged and the missed-savings estimate
Which renewals were competitively sourced vs rolled over last year
Data quality and completeness of existing contract records

p3_solution_approach_focus: Design the consolidated renewal calendar, the ranking of renewals by value and leverage, and the recommended-action logic with a human decision point.
p4_roadmap_value_focus: Size savings from proactively managed renewals versus the auto-renew baseline; prioritize the highest-value, highest-leverage renewals first.
p5_execution_focus: Run the renewal pipeline live, route selected renewals into competitive sourcing or renegotiation, and track captured savings in a regular cadence.

business_outcome: Corporate shared services get an evidence-based view of how key suppliers perform across operating companies, so Lakeshore can hold suppliers accountable, focus improvement on the worst performers, and use consolidated leverage in negotiations.
current_state_work_problem: Supplier performance is judged anecdotally and separately by each operating company. The same supplier may be praised in one and criticized in another with no shared record. Delivery, quality, and service data sit in different systems, so there is no consistent scorecard and no consolidated view to drive supplier reviews or negotiations.
phase_one_solution_approach: Build a supplier performance intelligence layer that pulls available delivery, quality, spend, and issue data into a consistent scorecard per supplier, consolidated across operating companies. A procurement lead reviews and interprets the scorecard for business reviews; the tool surfaces insights but doesn't score suppliers as final fact or trigger actions. Feeds Tower for value and negotiation leverage.

building_blocks_not_yet.reason: Automated supplier actions (holds, penalties, escalations) require trusted, complete data and clear policy; unsafe until scorecards are validated.
Formal supplier-consequence governance is a later layer; phase one is about visibility, not enforcement.
A supplier-review copilot is useful later but depends on a trusted scorecard foundation first.

required_p2_evidence: Available delivery, quality, and service data per supplier across operating companies
Current spend by supplier consolidated across the group
Examples of how supplier reviews are run today and what data they use
Known data gaps and inconsistencies across operating-company systems
Which suppliers are strategic / highest-spend and shared across operating companies
p2_current_state_focus: Understand what performance data actually exists, how reliable it is, and how supplier reviews are conducted today across operating companies.
p3_solution_approach_focus: Design the consistent supplier scorecard, the consolidated cross-operating-company view, and how a lead interprets insights in reviews.
p4_roadmap_value_focus: Justify the move on better negotiation leverage, focused supplier improvement, and consolidated spend visibility; start with strategic, shared suppliers.
p5_execution_focus: Use scorecards live in supplier business reviews, track performance improvement and negotiation outcomes, and refine data sources in a regular cadence.

Performance improvement in worst-performing suppliers over time
Consolidated spend visibility across operating companies
Negotiation savings enabled by performance evidence
Number of supplier reviews run on shared data

Clear labeling of data confidence and gaps on each scorecard
Audit trail of data sources feeding each score
Fair-treatment guardrails so incomplete data doesn't unfairly penalize a supplier
Confidentiality of supplier-specific performance data
client_stakeholders: Corporate VP of Procurement / Shared Services
what_good_looks_like: One consistent, evidence-based scorecard per strategic supplier consolidated across operating companies, clearly showing data confidence, used to run sharper supplier reviews and negotiate from consolidated leverage.
biggest_risks_traps: Data is patchy and inconsistent across operating companies, undermining scorecard credibility
Comparing suppliers on unequal data can be unfair and damage relationships
Leads may treat AI-surfaced scores as objective truth rather than a starting point
