No standard way to show and act on data-confidence levels so weak data isn't over-trusted
Fair-comparison guardrails for suppliers with uneven data are not part of the model

business_outcome: Lakeshore's corporate shared services get visibility and light-touch control over the long tail of low-value, fragmented purchases across operating companies, so off-contract 'maverick' buying is reduced, spend is steered to preferred suppliers, and savings are captured on spend that today gets no procurement attention.
current_state_work_problem: A large share of purchases are small, one-off, and made outside preferred contracts by many buyers across operating companies. Nobody has time to manage this tail, so the group pays more than it should, uses too many suppliers for the same category, and can't see where off-contract buying is happening or why.
phase_one_solution_approach: Build an analytics layer that classifies and consolidates tail spend across operating companies, surfaces where buying goes off preferred contracts, and recommends where to steer purchases or consolidate suppliers. A procurement analyst reviews the patterns and decides on interventions (guidance, catalog changes, supplier consolidation); the tool recommends and does not block or redirect purchases automatically. Consolidation candidates feed AbarVa's Source surface and savings feed Tower.

building_blocks_not_yet.reason: Automatically blocking or redirecting purchases risks disrupting operations; phase one steers behavior through guidance and catalogs, not hard automation.
A per-transaction review agent isn't warranted at tail-spend volumes yet; phase one works at the pattern level, not transaction by transaction.
Formal purchasing-policy enforcement is a later step once patterns and preferred-supplier guidance are established.

required_p2_evidence: Full spend data across operating companies with supplier and category detail
Definition of preferred contracts and catalogs today
Estimate of spend going off-contract and to fragmented suppliers
Buyer population and how tail purchases are made today
Data-quality assessment of spend categorization
p2_current_state_focus: Quantify the size and shape of tail spend, how much is off-contract, and where fragmentation and price leakage are worst.
p3_solution_approach_focus: Design the spend classification, the off-contract detection, the recommended interventions, and how analysts act on them without disrupting operations.
p4_roadmap_value_focus: Size savings from consolidation and on-contract steering; prioritize the categories with the most fragmented, highest-leakage tail spend.
p5_execution_focus: Run tail-spend interventions live (catalog updates, supplier consolidation, buyer guidance), track on-contract rate and savings, and review in a regular cadence.
tower_metrics: Percent of spend on preferred contracts (on-contract rate)
Reduction in supplier count for consolidated categories
Share of tail spend with clear category visibility
Off-contract spend trend across operating companies
required_controls: Human decision on every intervention before it affects buyers
Clear labeling of spend-classification confidence
Audit trail of recommended and implemented interventions
Guardrails so steering doesn't disrupt urgent or operational purchases
Confidentiality of operating-company spend detail
client_stakeholders: Corporate VP of Procurement / Shared Services
what_good_looks_like: Shared services can see the whole tail of spend across operating companies, know where off-contract buying happens, and steer purchases to preferred suppliers with clear savings, turning previously ignored spend into managed savings.
biggest_risks_traps: Poor spend classification produces misleading tail-spend numbers
Over-aggressive steering frustrates buyers and pushes them further off-system
Savings estimates may be optimistic without finance validation and a baseline
Operating-company autonomy makes central steering politically hard
gaps_in_current_moves_model: Spend-classification data readiness is a large hidden effort the Moves model doesn't scope cleanly within the move
No standard baseline-and-attribution method to make tail-spend savings claims defensible to finance
Change-management for buyer behavior across autonomous operating companies is under-modeled

business_outcome: Employee and manager questions and issues reaching the shared-services HR team are understood, prioritized, and routed to the right specialist or operating-company HR partner on first touch, cutting time-to-first-response and reducing cases that bounce between teams.
current_state_work_problem: HR shared services at Lakeshore receives a mixed inbound stream (email, portal tickets, phone follow-ups) spanning payroll, benefits, leave, workplace concerns, and manager queries across several operating companies. Cases are manually read, categorized, and assigned by a small intake team. Categories are inconsistent, urgent or sensitive matters (harassment, ADA, whistleblower) are sometimes missed in the queue, and cross-operating-company cases get misrouted, driving rework and slow response.
phase_one_solution_approach: A human-in-the-loop triage assistant that reads each incoming case, proposes a category, urgency, sensitivity flag, and suggested owner/operating company, and drafts a first-response acknowledgement. An intake specialist confirms or corrects every routing decision before it takes effect. Sensitive categories are always escalated to a named human, never auto-closed. No adverse or eligibility decision is ever made by the assistant.

building_blocks_not_yet.reason: Auto-routing without a human confirming the owner is unsafe while category accuracy is unproven and sensitive-case handling must stay with people; automate only after triage accuracy is measured over a pilot.
Phase one should sit on top of the existing HR case tool rather than replacing it; a platform change is a later decision once the triage model earns trust.

required_p2_evidence: A representative sample of past cases with their true category, urgency, and correct owner, agreed with HR intake leads
The current category and routing rules used across operating companies, and where they conflict
Definitions of sensitive case types (harassment, ADA/accommodation, whistleblower, investigations) and their mandated handling paths
Baseline metrics: current time-to-first-response, misroute rate, and reopen/bounce rate
Data privacy and retention rules for HR case content, including who may see what across operating companies
p2_current_state_focus: Map how cases actually flow today across operating companies, quantify misroutes and response delays, and document where sensitive matters must bypass any automation. Confirm what employee data the intake process legitimately touches.
p3_solution_approach_focus: Design the triage taxonomy, the confidence thresholds at which the assistant may suggest versus must defer, the mandatory human-review points, and the sensitive-case escalation path. Define what a good acknowledgement draft looks like and the specialist's confirm/correct interaction.
p4_roadmap_value_focus: Size the value from faster first response and fewer misroutes, phase the rollout operating-company by operating-company, and build the business case against current intake effort and reopen cost.
p5_execution_focus: Run the assistant in suggest-only mode with specialists confirming every routing, track accuracy and correction rate weekly, and expand categories only as accuracy holds.
required_controls: Every routing decision confirmed by a human before it takes effect during pilot
Sensitive categories always escalated to a named person and never auto-closed
Access to case content scoped by operating company and role
Full audit trail of suggested versus final routing for every case
No eligibility, disciplinary, or adverse decision made by the assistant
client_stakeholders: Works council / employee representatives where applicable
what_good_looks_like: Cases are correctly categorized and routed on first touch the large majority of the time, sensitive matters reach the right specialist immediately, first-response time drops materially, and intake specialists spend their time resolving rather than sorting — with a clear audit trail behind every routing decision.
biggest_risks_traps: A sensitive case (harassment, ADA, whistleblower) mis-categorized as routine and buried in a general queue
Employee case content crossing operating-company boundaries it should not
Specialists rubber-stamping suggestions once volume rises, eroding the human-in-the-loop safeguard
Taxonomy that looks clean in design but does not match how employees actually phrase issues
Perception among employees that a machine is judging their HR issue
gaps_in_current_moves_model: No built-in notion of a 'sensitive item must bypass automation' rule as a first-class control on a building block
Value tracking assumes clean baselines; HR intake baselines are often not instrumented before the Move starts
The model does not yet express confidence-threshold gating (suggest vs. defer) as a designable parameter

business_outcome: Managers across Lakeshore's operating companies get consistent, compliant, market-aligned job descriptions produced in hours rather than weeks, with a clean approval trail — speeding hiring and reducing inconsistency and legal exposure in postings.
current_state_work_problem: Each operating company writes job descriptions its own way. Managers copy old postings, language drifts, pay-transparency and equal-opportunity requirements are applied inconsistently, and levels/titles don't map to any shared framework. HR compliance reviews are manual, slow, and easy to skip, so postings go out with inconsistent or non-compliant language.
phase_one_solution_approach: A drafting assistant that generates a first job-description draft from a manager's inputs (role, level, must-haves) grounded in Lakeshore's approved templates, job-level framework, and required legal language. The manager edits, then it routes through a defined HR/compliance approval before publishing. The assistant drafts; humans own every approval. It flags missing pay-transparency or EEO language rather than silently inserting decisions.

building_blocks_not_yet.reason: A clean shared job-level and title framework may not exist yet across operating companies; if it's missing, that becomes its own upstream effort rather than something to assume in phase one.
Market-benchmark and pay-equity analytics on postings are valuable but a later layer once consistent, well-structured descriptions exist to analyze.
Worth adding once volume is real; early on the win is qualitative consistency and speed, measurable but not yet a standing cadence.

required_p2_evidence: Lakeshore's approved job-description templates and any shared job-level / title framework
Required legal language by jurisdiction (pay transparency, EEO, accommodation statements)
A sample of recent postings showing current inconsistency and compliance gaps
The real approval chain for postings in each operating company
Baseline time-to-post and rework/return rate on descriptions
p2_current_state_focus: Document how descriptions are actually created and approved today, where compliant language is missing, and whether a usable shared level/title framework exists or must be built.
p3_solution_approach_focus: Design the input form managers fill, the grounding sources the draft must use, the compliance checks the assistant must surface, and the approval routing and sign-off record.
p4_roadmap_value_focus: Quantify time saved and compliance-risk reduction, sequence rollout by operating company and job family, and decide whether a shared level framework is a prerequisite workstream.
p5_execution_focus: Publish only through the approval workflow, monitor edit-distance and rejection reasons to improve drafts, and track adoption by managers.
tower_metrics: Consistency score against the shared framework
required_controls: No description published without the defined HR/compliance approval
Required legal language flagged and confirmed present, never silently auto-inserted as a decision
Jurisdiction-specific requirements applied based on posting location
Full record of who approved each description and when
Templates and legal language are versioned and centrally owned
what_good_looks_like: A manager describes a role in minutes, gets a clean draft grounded in Lakeshore's framework with the right legal language already flagged, edits lightly, and it moves through approval and to posting fast — with descriptions looking consistent across operating companies and audit-ready.
biggest_risks_traps: Missing or wrong jurisdiction-specific pay-transparency or EEO language creating legal exposure
Bias or non-inclusive language slipping into drafts and being copied at scale
No shared level framework, so 'consistency' has nothing to anchor to
Managers bypassing the tool and posting old descriptions anyway
Approval step treated as a formality and skipped under hiring pressure
gaps_in_current_moves_model: The model treats a prerequisite like 'shared job-level framework exists' as an assumption rather than surfacing it as a gating dependency at P2
No first-class way to express jurisdiction-conditional required content as a control
Bias/inclusive-language review isn't represented as a distinct check the design must include

business_outcome: Employees and managers get fast, accurate, source-cited answers to HR policy questions (leave, benefits, expenses, conduct) tailored to their operating company and location, deflecting routine questions from the HR service center and reducing inconsistent guidance.
current_state_work_problem: Policies differ by operating company and jurisdiction, live in scattered handbooks and intranet pages, and are often outdated. Employees can't tell which version applies to them, so they email HR or ask managers, who sometimes guess. The HR service center is flooded with repetitive policy questions, and inconsistent answers create fairness and compliance risk.
phase_one_solution_approach: A retrieval copilot that answers policy questions only from Lakeshore's current, approved policy documents, always shows the source and effective date, and scopes answers to the employee's operating company and location. When policy is unclear, conflicting, or the question touches an individual's situation (leave eligibility, discipline, accommodation), it hands off to a human rather than answering. It informs; it does not decide entitlements.

building_blocks_not_yet.reason: Determining an individual's eligibility or entitlement is a decision that must stay with HR; phase one answers general policy only and hands individual cases to people.
Triggering downstream actions (e.g., filing a leave request) from an answer is premature until answer accuracy and hand-off boundaries are proven.

required_p2_evidence: The authoritative, current set of policies per operating company and jurisdiction, with owners and effective dates
A list of known outdated, duplicate, or conflicting policy documents to remediate
The most common policy questions and today's answer sources
Clear boundaries of what counts as general policy vs. an individual entitlement decision
Baseline volume of policy questions hitting the service center and current answer accuracy/consistency
p2_current_state_focus: Establish which policy documents are truly authoritative and current, find the conflicts and stale versions, and define the line between answerable general policy and questions that must go to a human.
p3_solution_approach_focus: Design source-grounding and mandatory citation, operating-company/jurisdiction scoping, the confidence and topic rules that trigger human hand-off, and the phrasing that avoids sounding like an entitlement decision.
p4_roadmap_value_focus: Size deflection of routine questions and consistency gains, and scope the policy-cleanup effort as an explicit prerequisite investment.
p5_execution_focus: Launch on a limited, well-governed policy set, monitor answer accuracy and hand-off rate, feed unanswered/incorrect questions back into policy remediation, and expand coverage as content is cleaned.
tower_metrics: Policy-question deflection rate from the service center
Correct hand-off rate on out-of-scope/individual questions
required_controls: Answers only from approved, current policy sources — no free-form generation of policy
Every answer shows its source and effective date
Answers scoped to the employee's operating company and jurisdiction
Individual-situation and unclear questions handed to a human, never answered as entitlement
Stale/conflicting content quarantined until remediated
what_good_looks_like: An employee asks a policy question, gets a clear answer scoped to their operating company with the exact source and effective date, and trusts it — while anything touching their individual entitlement is smoothly handed to HR. Routine question volume to the service center drops and answers are consistent everywhere.
biggest_risks_traps: Answering from an outdated or wrong-jurisdiction policy and giving employees false assurance
Drifting from 'here's the policy' into 'here's your entitlement,' which is a decision HR must own
Content debt: without policy cleanup, the copilot confidently cites contradictory documents
Employees treating the answer as binding when it should point to HR for their case
Coverage gaps read as authoritative silence
gaps_in_current_moves_model: The heavy upstream policy-remediation dependency is easy to under-scope; the model doesn't force sizing it before promising deflection
No first-class 'answer vs. decide' boundary control that this use case critically needs
Currency/effective-date of source content isn't represented as a tracked quality gate

business_outcome: New hires across Lakeshore's operating companies are productive on day one because every onboarding task — accounts, access, equipment, payroll setup, compliance training, manager check-ins — is triggered, tracked, and completed on time, with nothing dropped between HR, IT, facilities, and the operating company.
current_state_work_problem: Onboarding spans HR, IT, facilities, payroll, and the hiring operating company, coordinated by checklists and email. Tasks fall through the cracks, new hires arrive without laptops or system access, compliance training lapses go unnoticed, and no one has a single view of onboarding status. It varies widely by operating company and depends on individual coordinators remembering steps.
phase_one_solution_approach: A workflow that generates the right onboarding task list for each new hire based on role, operating company, and location, assigns tasks to the correct owners, tracks completion, and surfaces a live status view with reminders and escalations for anything overdue. Humans still perform the tasks and sign off on compliance-critical steps; the orchestration coordinates and chases rather than granting access or clearing requirements itself.

building_blocks_not_yet.reason: Phase one should orchestrate across existing HR, IT, and payroll systems rather than deploy a new onboarding platform; consolidation is a later decision once the flow is proven.
Access provisioning and compliance clearance are governed decisions that must stay with their owners; the assistant coordinates, it does not grant access or waive requirements.

required_p2_evidence: The full onboarding task set by role, operating company, and location, and who owns each task
Which systems must be touched (identity/access, payroll, learning, equipment) and how status can be read from them
Compliance-critical steps that legally must be completed before start or within a window
Baseline: on-time completion rate, day-one readiness rate, and where tasks currently drop
Access-governance rules — separation of duties, approvals required before provisioning
p2_current_state_focus: Map the real end-to-end onboarding flow across all owners and systems, quantify where and how often it breaks, and pin down the compliance-critical steps that cannot be missed.
p3_solution_approach_focus: Design role/company-specific task generation, ownership and assignment rules, the reminder/escalation logic, the live status view, and which steps require human sign-off before the hire proceeds.
p4_roadmap_value_focus: Quantify day-one readiness gains and coordinator time saved, and sequence rollout by operating company and role type.
p5_execution_focus: Run the orchestration live with owners still executing tasks, track on-time completion and day-one readiness weekly, and tune task templates from misses and escalations.
tower_metrics: Day-one readiness rate (all critical tasks complete at start)
required_controls: Access and account provisioning still executed and approved by their governed owners, not by the orchestrator
Compliance-critical steps explicitly signed off before a hire is marked ready
Separation-of-duties and approval rules preserved for provisioning
Full audit trail of task status, owners, and sign-offs per hire
New-hire personal data scoped to the operating company and roles that need it
what_good_looks_like: Every new hire's tasks are generated automatically for their role and operating company, each owner knows exactly what to do and by when, overdue items escalate before they become day-one failures, and HR has one live view of readiness — with access and compliance steps still owned and signed off by the right people.
biggest_risks_traps: Treating orchestration as authority to grant access, breaking access-governance and separation of duties
A compliance-critical step (e.g., mandated safety or background check) marked done without real sign-off
Status that looks green because a system integration is stale, not because work is actually done
Task templates that don't reflect real operating-company differences, so the list is wrong
New-hire personal data over-shared across owners and operating companies
gaps_in_current_moves_model: The model doesn't cleanly separate 'coordinate a task' from 'have authority to complete it,' which is the core safety line here
Status accuracy depends on reading other systems' state, and integration-freshness isn't a tracked quality gate in the model
Compliance-critical sign-off as a hard gate isn't a first-class control concept

use_case: Leave and accommodation intake and status assistant
business_outcome: Employees requesting leave (FMLA, medical, parental) or a workplace accommodation get a clear, guided intake and reliable status updates, while the sensitive eligibility and accommodation decisions stay firmly with HR specialists — reducing errors, delays, and compliance risk across operating companies.
current_state_work_problem: Leave and accommodation requests are among the most sensitive and legally exposed HR processes, and at Lakeshore they vary by operating company and jurisdiction. Employees don't know what to submit, requests stall waiting on missing documentation, status is opaque so employees repeatedly chase HR, and inconsistent handling across operating companies creates real FMLA/ADA compliance and fairness risk.
phase_one_solution_approach: An assistant that guides the employee through what a given leave or accommodation request needs, checks that required documentation is present, explains general process and timelines with sources, and gives status updates — while every eligibility and accommodation decision, and all medical information, is handled by an HR specialist. It collects and informs; it never determines eligibility, approves leave, or interprets medical information. Sensitive health data is tightly restricted.

building_blocks_not_yet.reason: Leave eligibility and accommodation determinations are legally sensitive, individualized decisions that must stay entirely with HR specialists and counsel — the assistant must not suggest outcomes.
Aggregate leave/accommodation analytics are valuable for capacity and equity but must wait until data handling and privacy controls are proven and access is tightly scoped.
Phase one guides intake and status on top of existing leave administration; replacing the system of record for a legally exposed process is a later, deliberate decision.

required_p2_evidence: Leave and accommodation types and their legal requirements by jurisdiction (FMLA, ADA, state leave, parental)
Required documentation and timelines per request type
The strict boundary between guidance/intake and any eligibility or medical determination
How and where sensitive medical information is stored and who may access it
Baseline: request cycle time, documentation-completeness rate, and status-chasing volume to HR
p2_current_state_focus: Map each leave/accommodation type's legal requirements and current handling across operating companies, and rigorously define what the assistant may touch versus what must stay with specialists and counsel — especially around medical information.
p3_solution_approach_focus: Design the guided intake, documentation checks, source-cited general-process answers, secure hand-off to specialists, and status updates — with hard walls around eligibility decisions and medical data.
p4_roadmap_value_focus: Size faster, more complete intake and reduced status-chasing, and scope the strict privacy and access controls as non-negotiable prerequisites.
p5_execution_focus: Pilot in one operating company with specialists owning all decisions, monitor documentation-completeness and cycle time, and confirm zero decisioning or medical-data leakage before expanding.
tower_metrics: On-time compliance with statutory leave timelines
Employee experience score for the leave/accommodation process
required_controls: Assistant never determines eligibility, approves leave, or interprets medical information
Sensitive medical data segregated with strict, minimal, audited access
Jurisdiction-specific legal requirements enforced and surfaced to specialists
Every request handed to a named HR specialist for decision, with full audit trail
Employee data scoped to the operating company and specialists handling the case
what_good_looks_like: An employee is guided to submit a complete leave or accommodation request the first time, always knows where it stands, and reaches a specialist quickly — while every eligibility and accommodation decision and all medical information stay with trained HR people under strict privacy controls, consistently across operating companies.
biggest_risks_traps: The assistant drifting into implying an eligibility outcome — a serious legal and fairness breach
Any mishandling or over-exposure of sensitive medical/health information
Inconsistent jurisdiction handling creating FMLA/ADA compliance violations
Employees perceiving automation in a deeply personal process as cold or dismissive
Guidance mistaken for a decision, creating false expectations and disputes
gaps_in_current_moves_model: The model has no first-class concept of a hard 'never decide / never interpret medical data' wall that this use case absolutely requires
Handling of specially protected data categories (medical/health) isn't represented as a distinct control tier
Phase-one realism suffers because the model doesn't force the privacy/legal prerequisites to be sized before the Move is greenlit

business_outcome: Cut the time and effort corporate shared services spends running periodic access reviews across operating-company systems, while raising the quality and auditability of every recertification decision so entitlements that should be revoked actually get revoked on time.
current_state_work_problem: Every quarter, corporate IT security pulls entitlement extracts from dozens of systems across Lakeshore's operating companies, formats them into spreadsheets, and emails them to hundreds of manager-reviewers. Reviewers rubber-stamp long lists they don't understand, context on what each entitlement grants is missing, revocations get lost in email threads, and the audit team spends weeks chasing incomplete campaigns and reassembling proof that reviews actually happened.
phase_one_solution_approach: A reviewer-facing copilot that assembles each manager's recertification packet with plain-language context (what the access grants, when it was last used, peer comparison, risk flags) and recommends keep/revoke, while the human reviewer makes and signs every decision. Revocation requests are routed to system owners; the campaign's completeness and every decision are captured as tamper-evident audit evidence.

building_blocks_not_yet.reason: Auto-executing revocations against production systems is too risky at P1; certification decisions must stay human-signed and revocation execution stays a controlled, owner-approved step until trust and rollback are proven.
Replacing or standing up a new identity-governance platform is a multi-quarter program; P1 rides on top of existing entitlement extracts rather than re-platforming.
Some entitlement remediation is needed, but the first move focuses on decision quality; deep source-data cleanup is scoped as a follow-on once gaps are quantified.

required_p2_evidence: Current recertification campaign calendar, scope, and populations by operating company
Sample entitlement extracts from the top 5-10 in-scope systems
Last two campaigns' completion rates, cycle time, and overdue/exception counts
Audit and internal-control findings from prior access-review cycles
List of privileged/high-risk entitlement types and current owners/approvers
p2_current_state_focus: Map how recertification runs today end to end, quantify reviewer burden and rubber-stamp rate, and expose where revocations fall through and where audit evidence is thin or missing.
p3_solution_approach_focus: Design the reviewer packet, the recommendation logic and its risk flags, the human sign-off and revocation-routing flow, and the evidence trail — being explicit that recommendations are advisory and every decision is human-owned.
p4_roadmap_value_focus: Quantify reviewer hours saved, cycle-time reduction, and reduction in overdue/stale access; phase rollout system-by-system starting with highest-risk populations; build the business case on audit-readiness and reduced access risk.
p5_execution_focus: Run live campaigns on a recurring cadence, track completion and revocation follow-through, monitor recommendation quality against reviewer overrides, and report audit-readiness to the control owners each cycle.
tower_metrics: Revocation follow-through rate (approved revocations actually executed)
required_controls: Human sign-off required on every keep/revoke decision
Segregation of duties between reviewer, system owner, and revocation executor
Tamper-evident audit trail of decisions, timestamps, and reviewers
Access controls limiting who can see entitlement data by operating company
Recommendation logic documented and reviewable by audit
client_stakeholders: IT Security / Identity & Access Management lead
what_good_looks_like: Campaigns close on time with every decision human-signed and context-rich, revocations demonstrably execute, and audit pulls a complete evidence pack in minutes instead of chasing spreadsheets for weeks.
biggest_risks_traps: Copilot recommendations quietly become the decision (rubber-stamping just moves upstream) unless override behavior is monitored
Revocation routing that stops at 'requested' but never confirms execution leaves real access risk open
Entitlement data quality is worse than assumed, undermining recommendation trust
Over-automation pressure from stakeholders wanting to auto-revoke before controls are proven
gaps_in_current_moves_model: Model has no first-class notion of a recurring compliance campaign with a completion SLA versus a one-time deliverable
No native concept of 'requested vs. executed vs. verified' state for a downstream remediation action
Evidence-integrity/tamper-evidence requirements aren't an explicit building-block attribute

business_outcome: Ensure that every employee and contractor across Lakeshore's operating companies attests to required corporate policies on time, with clean, defensible proof — reducing manual chasing by compliance staff and eliminating gaps that surface as audit findings.
current_state_work_problem: Corporate compliance tracks policy attestations (code of conduct, security policy, data handling, conflict-of-interest) in spreadsheets and disconnected tools per operating company. Distribution lists are stale, reminders are sent by hand, completion status is reconciled manually, and when audit or a regulator asks 'who attested to what version, when,' the team scrambles to reassemble evidence across systems and time periods.
phase_one_solution_approach: An intelligence and tracking layer that consolidates who-owes-what across operating companies, drafts targeted reminders for compliance staff to review and send, and flags at-risk populations — with a knowledge copilot that answers employee questions about the policy in plain language. Attestations and their exact policy version are captured as clean, timestamped evidence. Compliance owns campaign launch and escalation decisions.

building_blocks_not_yet.reason: Attestation is inherently the employee's own act; there's no delegated agent making decisions on their behalf, so a HITL agent block adds little at P1.
Attestation is largely a completeness-and-coverage problem, not a judgment call; decision-support is deferred until exception-handling patterns justify it.
Standing up a new attestation platform is heavier than needed at P1; the first move rides on existing HR/identity rosters and distribution mechanisms.

required_p2_evidence: Full list of required policies, current versions, and owning functions
Current attestation rosters and how population is derived per operating company
Last cycle's completion rates, overdue counts, and time-to-complete
Audit/regulatory findings tied to attestation gaps or version ambiguity
Current reminder/escalation process and who owns it
p2_current_state_focus: Establish the true required population per policy, quantify manual chasing effort and completion gaps, and expose where version-tracking and evidence are ambiguous.
p3_solution_approach_focus: Design the consolidated tracking view, the reminder/escalation flow with human launch control, the plain-language policy copilot, and the version-anchored evidence capture.

business_outcome: Speed up how corporate shared services collects, chases, and validates security and compliance evidence from Lakeshore's third parties (audits, certifications, insurance, questionnaires) so vendor risk reviews finish faster and no operating company onboards a vendor on stale or missing evidence.
current_state_work_problem: Third-party risk analysts email vendors for the same documents repeatedly, track responses in spreadsheets, manually read PDFs to find expiry dates and control coverage, and struggle to keep a current picture across hundreds of vendors shared by multiple operating companies. Evidence expires unnoticed, reviews stall waiting on documents, and the audit trail of what was collected and assessed is fragmented.
phase_one_solution_approach: A knowledge/retrieval copilot that reads submitted vendor evidence and surfaces key facts (certification scope, expiry, exceptions) for an analyst to verify, combined with automated outreach and follow-up to collect and refresh documents. Analysts make every risk determination; the intelligence layer keeps a live view of coverage and expiry, and all collected evidence and assessments form an auditable record.

Replacing the third-party risk management platform is out of scope for P1; the move augments existing intake and tracking rather than re-platforming.
Historical vendor-evidence backfill is valuable but sequenced after the live collection flow proves out, to avoid boiling the ocean.

business_outcome: Help corporate risk and control teams triage the flood of control exceptions and policy deviations across operating companies faster and more consistently, so genuine risks get to the right owner and decision quickly and low-risk noise doesn't clog the queue — without ever auto-approving an exception.
current_state_work_problem: Control exceptions and risk-acceptance requests arrive through inconsistent channels, are described in varying quality, and land in a shared queue. Analysts manually read each one, hunt for related policy and prior similar cases, guess at severity and routing, and often let low-risk items pile up while high-risk ones wait. Consistency across reviewers is poor and the rationale for how each exception was handled is inconsistently recorded.
phase_one_solution_approach: A copilot that, for each incoming exception, retrieves the relevant policy and similar prior cases, drafts a proposed severity and routing with rationale, and prepares the packet — while a human analyst confirms severity, routing, and any approval. Exceptions are never auto-approved; the copilot only organizes, contextualizes, and recommends. Every triage decision and its rationale are recorded as auditable evidence.

building_blocks_not_yet.reason: Auto-routing and especially any auto-disposition of exceptions is deferred; at P1 the human confirms severity and routing so no exception is closed or accepted without judgment.
Replacing the GRC/exception system is out of scope; the move augments the existing intake and queue rather than re-platforming.
Portfolio-level exception analytics is valuable but sequenced after triage quality is proven; P1 focuses on per-case triage, not trend dashboards.

p5_execution_focus: Run live triage on cadence, monitor triage time and analyst override rate, watch for high-severity items aging, and report consistency and audit-readiness to control owners.

use_case: Regulatory change monitoring and impact routing
business_outcome: Give corporate compliance a reliable early-warning and routing capability for regulatory and standards changes that affect Lakeshore's operating companies, so relevant changes reach the right control owner with a plain-language impact summary — reducing missed obligations and late, reactive scrambles.
current_state_work_problem: Compliance staff manually monitor a patchwork of regulators and standards bodies relevant to Lakeshore's varied industrial businesses, read dense updates, guess which operating companies and controls are affected, and forward things ad hoc. Changes are missed or noticed late, impact assessment is inconsistent, and there's no clean record showing the company saw a change and acted on it — a gap auditors and regulators probe.
phase_one_solution_approach: A knowledge/retrieval copilot that ingests regulatory and standards updates, summarizes each in plain language, and proposes which operating companies, policies, and control owners are potentially affected — for a compliance analyst to confirm and route. The analyst owns every relevance and impact judgment; the copilot triages and drafts. Each change, its assessment, and its routing form an auditable trail of awareness and response.

building_blocks_not_yet.reason: Auto-creating obligations or control changes from a detected update is deferred; a compliance human must confirm relevance and impact before anything is routed as an action at P1.
A regulatory-change portfolio dashboard is a fast-follow; P1 focuses on reliable detection, summarization, and routing of individual changes.
Standing up a full regulatory-change-management platform is heavier than needed; the first move augments existing monitoring and routing with better triage and evidence.

p4_roadmap_value_focus: Quantify monitoring hours saved, reduction in missed/late responses, and faster time-to-owner; sequence by regulatory domain and operating company; build the case on reduced regulatory exposure and demonstrable diligence.
p5_execution_focus: Run continuous monitoring, route confirmed changes to owners on cadence, track time-to-owner and closure of required responses, and maintain the auditable awareness trail.

what_good_looks_like: Relevant regulatory changes are caught early, summarized in plain English, and land with the right control owner within a defined window — with a clean, auditable record that Lakeshore saw each change and acted, and humans owning every impact call.
